content.summary_of_the_paper: For irregularly sampled time-series input, ODE-RNNs update their hidden state as the solution to an ODE. This results in the hidden state being represented by a continuous function in the time domain. But this continuity does not extend to other aspects of the ODEs such as input transition or other RNN specific latent variables such as reset, memory and forget gates. As a result, a jump mechanism is required to process new discrete input. This work extends this continuous notion to all the latent variables of a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) for the time-series inputs. It even interpolates the discrete time-series input observations to create a continuous representation in the time domain. Empirical evaluations against standard baselines on real-world datasets show non-trivial improvements.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
- As compared to ODE-RNNs that have continuous hidden states, it extends continuity in other latent variables and the input time-series
- It creates continuous GRU variant using Delay Differential Equations 

Weaknesses:
- Many details seem to missing (see below)
- Lack of ablations on the impact of the new components ( continuous vs discrete inputs, delay vs ordinary differential equations in ODE-RNNs, choice of the solver )

Questions for Authors:

(1) It is unclear what gains DDE brings as compared to standard ODE based transitions in the continuous GRUs? Are there any ablations that compare the following two schemes
  - (a) Continuous GRU ( including continuity in other latent variable and input ) + ODE
  - (b) Continuous GRU ( including continuity in other latent variable and input ) + DDE

(2) Why do you not utilize other ODE-RNNs for modelling the continuity? One can incorporate the notion of continuity in other existing ODE-RNNs? Besides some RNNs already have all the latent variables in continuous space (for ex. Time Adaptive RNNs https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2021/papers/Kag_Time_Adaptive_Recurrent_Neural_Network_CVPR_2021_paper.pdf ).

(3) How do you integrate continuous GRU in the problems at hand? Do you use a black-box ODE solver? or do you discretize the ODE and back-propagate through some discretization schemes? What is the impact of these aspects on the training/inference time?

(4) It is unclear as to how much gains proposed Continuous GRU obtains by simplying having a continuity in the input space (as done by the Cubic Hermite Spline interpolation method). It is entirely possible that the observed gains are due to the continuity only in the input time-series. If so, such scheme can be integrated in existing ODE-RNNs. Thus, it becomes very important to account for improvements due to various components.

(5) Need a thorough ablative analysis
  - black-box solver vs discretization 
  - DDE vs ODE 
  - input continuity vs continuity in all latent variables
  - input continuity with existing ODE-RNNs 

(6) Datasets used are somewhat small scale. How does the proposal scale to larger datasets with longer sequence lengths?


(7) How are these baselines trained ? How do you perform hyper-parameter tuning?

(8) Could you elaborate as to why baselines have larger training time than the proposed method? Does the same hold for inference time? Technically the proposed GRU should be more computationally expensive as it incorporates the continuity in all latent variables. In addition, it also need to create a continuous time-series by cubic hermite interpolation. So it is unclear why the training time is smaller.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
To the best of my knowledge, incorporating continuity in all the aspects of the GRU is novel. This includes continuity in the following aspects :  input, hidden state, reset, memory and forget gates. 

Evaluation is lacking as the work is missing many crucial ablations that would justify the design choices ( continuous vs discrete inputs, delay vs ordinary differential equations in ODE-RNNs, choice of the solver, is there even a need for continuity in hidden space? )

Missing references
      Continuous Time RNN (by Rosenblatt),
	Incremental RNNs (https://openreview.net/forum?id=HylpqA4FwS), 
	Antisymmetric RNN : https://openreview.net/forum?id=ryxepo0cFX
 	Deep Equilibrium Models (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.01377.pdf)
	CoRNN : https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00951.pdf
      Time Adaptive RNNs (https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2021/papers/Kag_Time_Adaptive_Recurrent_Neural_Network_CVPR_2021_paper.pdf)
content.summary_of_the_review: Integrating the notion of continuity in all aspects of the GRU (input / hidden state / gates) is novel. This paper does not justify all the design choices made to construct such a continuous GRU variant (see weaknesses). It is also unclear if such a design choice comes with significant computational overhead (train/inference).
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a model that continuously generalises all the parts of Gated Recurrent Units, by rewriting the hidden state and gates differential equations as delay differential equations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Clean, clear and concise presentation
- Bringing GRUs to the realm of fully continuous networks is an important theoretical step

Weaknesses:
- Although this paper offers a necessary contribution towards completeness in the field of continuous time sequential modelling networks, there are doubts about the architecture's ability to compete with state of the art sequence modeling models.
- The baselines chosen are either previous versions of GRU architectures or variants of Neural ODEs. The datasets are also not challenging in terms of length and complexity of the data. It thus seems that the authors only show increased expressivity of ContGRU over a subset of models of specific nature. Current state-of-the-art RNN memory capabilities for sequence modelling (see works such as "Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces" by Gu et al, and "Liquid Structural State-Space Models" by Hasani, Lechner et al), allow successful learning of Long Range Arena tasks such as Path-X (16384 sequence length). How does ContGRU compare to such benchmarks?
- The additional need for input data interpolation.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is very well written and enjoyable to read. Reproducibility is ensured with the sharing of baselines and all the hyperparameter settings used for experiments as well as an explanation document.
Although translating models from the discrete to continuous realm is a very common exercise in the community (as documented by the authors), the handling of gates through DDEs is an interesting new direction although it comes with the (somewhat undesirable) price of input interpolation preprocessing.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper offers an interesting approach to fully continuously generalise all the part of the highly popular GRU architecture. The use of DDEs to achieve this end does seem to enhance expressivity without heavy compromising on computation time. Although the performance results of ContGRU lack state of the art impressiveness on difficult sequence modelling tasks, the theoretical design itself is of enough interest.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a fully continuous GRU by representing its hidden state and other gates as delay differential equations. They first generate a continuous path x(t) from discrete observations via interpolation algorithms and then model r(t), z(t), g(t), and h(t) of GRUs as an augmented DDE to continuously produce all the parts of GRUs. In addition, this paper evaluates their method on three real-world datasets compared with 13 baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
1. The proposed method is the first-ever model that continuously generalizes all the components of GRUs, including the hidden state and various gates. 
2. The paper is well-organized. The paper is mostly easy to follow. 
3. The experiment results are promising, and an extensive set of prevalent time series forecasting models are compared. 

Weaknesses: 
1. My major concern is that the difference between Neural controlled differential equations [1] and the proposed model is not well illustrated. In my view, the proposed model seems a combination of GRUs and NCDEs. Once the continuous path x(t) is generated, how to use it in the later process? Since x(t) is only mentioned in Sec. 3.1 overall workflows but not in equations in 3.2. It would be good if there is a section thoroughly comparing the NCDE and the proposed method. And more details of the role of the continuous path x(t) are needed. 
2. Another question is the speed of computations. Why the proposed model is much faster than NCDE-based baselines (more than 10 times in forecasting weather experiments)? Intuitively, more continuous components in GRUs may slow down the computations and thus lead to longer training time. In addition, it seems questionable that ODE-RNN is much faster than NCDE-based models, which is opposite to the finding in [1], where NCDE was only slightly faster than the ODE-RNN model. 
3. The motivation is a bit unclear. Why do we need to make all parts of GRUs fully continuous? What’s the shortcoming of the jump mechanism? It will be more understandable if the motivation and the research gap can be discussed and analyzed deeper. 


Reference: 
[1] Kidger, P., Morrill, J., Foster, J., & Lyons, T. (2020). Neural controlled differential equations for irregular time series. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33, 6696-6707.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is mostly well-written. The technical quality is solid but the novelty and motivation should be further justified.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the above comments, I believe this paper still has large space to improve. Thus I vote for a borderline rejection in this round.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a Continuous GRU (Cont-GRU) method as a generalization of GRU to continuous time, with applications to processing irregular time series. The main methodological contribution is to generalize the GRU to continuous time, especially the GRU components such as the reset gate, update gate, and update vector.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper provides a good related work and strong collection of baselines for all experimental results. However, the paper's method is confusingly described and does not appear to have substantial significance. To my understanding, there are two main components of the proposed method:

**Fully continuous model**
The paper repeatedly emphasizes that past methods are only jump-continuous in time instead of fully continuous in the hidden state, and moreover that continuous generalizations of components outside the hidden state (such as the GRU gates) have not had a continuous generalization. The justification provided is
> GRU-ODE-Bayes does not calculate the time derivatives of the reset gate, the update gate, and the update vector, denoted $\frac{d\mathbf{r}(t)}{dt}$, $\frac{d\mathbf{z}(t)}{dt}$, and $\frac{d\mathbf{g}(t)}{dt}$ respectively, since the input time series sample $\{(\mathbf{x}_i, t_i)\}$ is discrete and it is impossible to calculate $\frac{d\mathbf{x}(t)}{dt}$.

Ultimately, all that is necessary to resolve the problem is to make $x(t)$ continuous instead of discrete, and the paper accomplishes this with a separate pre-processing step to interpolate the input $x_i$ to $x(t)$. This is not a significant methodological contribution. Moreover, the paper is not very transparent about this being the crux of the problem, nor does it discuss the related methods well - for example, this has been done before, such as in the NCDE line of works, which share all the same "fully continuous" properties as the proposed model but are not discussed in the introduction.

**Delay Differential Equation**
Another interesting part of the method that is not as common is the DDE aspect. However, the motivation for introducing this variation in the differential equation is not clear (equation (3)); what benefits does it provide? Moreover, the actual change to the method is confusing (equation (4)). It seems like this is the same as a normal GRU except replacing a constant $1$ by a new term $\Delta t$, which is not motivated or defined.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper can use major improvement to clarity, quality, and novelty. In addition to the above points, the following are some additional comments:

1. As mentioned above, the entire method rests on the interpolation of the discrete data $x_i$ to a continuous input $x(t)$, yet this critical interpolation step is not discussed in more detail. For example, what is the interpolation method used?
2. Algorithm 1 box does not provide any value.
3. Forecasting experiment (Section 4.3): experimental protocol is very unclear. What are the training data and targets? Is it a one-step prediction or multi-step rollout? Figure 3 is hard to interpret because the training details are not provided; for example, why are all methods inaccurate at the beginning of the window (usually forecasting is conditioned on some past data so one would expect the methods to get ground truth at the left side of the window)?
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a new method in the family of continuous RNNs. However, the method seems to rest entirely on a simple interpolation step during preprocessing that is not well described or positioned.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a novel continuous-time formulation of a GRU, which is inspired by delay differential equations (DDEs). Further several interpolation algorithms are considered for fitting a continuous function to the time series samples. In turn, this interpolation algorithm is used to predict the missing discrete time points in the sequence of interest. The performance of the resulting model is demonstrated on 3 different sequential tasks, demonstrating improved performance compared to a range of state-of-the-art models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The ideas presented (i.e., time-delays, and interpolation algorithms for fitting the input sequences) are plausible, and novel. Further, the experimental results are good, but limited. My main concern is that the paper does not provide any deeper insights into `why’ the model achieves better performance. This could be for instance addressed by providing a detailed ablation study that breaks apart the components and studies the individual performance. Further, I have several other questions: 

* How do you select $\tau$, and how sensitive is the model to different values of $\tau$. I assume that delay can introduce numerical instabilities.  

* The paper does not provide any stability results for the proposed GRU. It would be good to better understand the long-term behavior of the proposed gated recurrent unit. This should be straight forward since you have formulated the model in continuous time. More generally, any discussion on vanishing and exploding gradients is missing.  

* Solving DDEs is typically more challenging than solving ODEs. I cannot find any discussion about this. Also, I cannot find any details about the numerical scheme that is used for learning the weights. This said, is the same numerical scheme used for all the baselines that you are comparing the performance with? 

* As mentioned above, since you propose several innovations, it is not clear which components lead to the improvements, or whether it is the combination. How does one of the other baselines methods perform when you combine it with your interpolation scheme? How does the proposed cont-GRU model perform without the interpolation scheme?  

* How does the proposed model perform on longer sequences? All the tasks considered involve only relatively short input sequences. 

* The training protocol / tuning parameter setting is a bit questionable. First, it is common practice in the RNN literature to fix the hidden dimensions across all models that are compared. Then you can show in addition the performance for smaller or bigger units. Thus, for the USHCN I would like to see experiments with the same hidden size that is used for the baseline. How are the baseline models doing here with smaller hidden units? Similar this should be shown for the PHYSIONET SEPSIS task. Just to clarify, do you use the same tuning parameters for all baseline models? (It is questionable to consider the same tuning parameters for such a wide range of different baseline models, each model should be fine-tuned for a fair comparison.) 

* I like the forecasting task, but why would you have missing values for stock prices? Again, the considered input sequence is very short. 

* There exists a large number of classic works on the intersection of DDEs and neural networks. It would be good to acknowledge some of these older works.

 Some minor comments: 

* A discussion of state-of-the art continuous-time RNNs is missing, see for instance [1,2,3] and related works therein. These models should be mentioned in the related works, and I think that they should be able to mode irregular sampled data as well. 

* Differential Eqauation-based models -> Differential Equation-based models 

* Can you comment on the train/ validation /test splits that you are using? It is common practice to put aside some of the datapoints from the train set to form a validation set. But I saw in your code that you split the test set into a validation and new test set. Maybe that is common practice for the datasets under consideration, but I am just wondering about it. Since you train / test all the models on the same split, it doesn’t matter too much. 

 
[1] Kag, Anil, Ziming Zhang, and Venkatesh Saligrama. "Rnns incrementally evolving on an equilibrium manifold: A panacea for vanishing and exploding gradients?." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2019. 

[2] Rusch, T. Konstantin, and Siddhartha Mishra. "Coupled Oscillatory Recurrent Neural Network (coRNN): An accurate and (gradient) stable architecture for learning long time dependencies." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2020. 

[3] Rusch, T. Konstantin, et al. "Long Expressive Memory for Sequence Modeling." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The presentation of the proposed methods appears a bit ad-hoc. It would be nice to see a better motivation for the proposed methods, and some theory that provides some interesting insights. Presenting only 3 experiments is somewhat weak for an experimental paper. It is not clear how the proposed model performs on problems with longer input sequences. The quality of the presentation is in parts a bit weak, i.e., there are several typos, and some of the sentences are difficult to parse. The organization can be improved. The discussion in section 3 needs to be expanded, in particular Section 3.2 is more or less just a laundry list of equations without much discussion.  Overall, the proposed results are novel, and code is provided for reproducing the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper introduces some interesting and novel ideas, but I don't feel that the paper is mature enough in its current form for publication. I can see that the cont-GRU has some potential, and it performs really well on the considered tasks. But it is not clear why the proposed model performs so well. Is it because the con-GRU is better fine tuned, or is there something else going on? A detailed ablation study can provide important insights to better understand the interplay of the proposed components. In turn, this understanding will help to foster and inspire new research directions. Lastly, the presentation of the method and the quality of writing needs to be improved.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
